title: The Dawn Patrol, the Pittsburgh Courier and Fuller
summary: Tex explains the Courier-sponsored Dawn Patrol of after-midnight club hopping, the black-owned bar scene before integration, and how a cosmetics salesman named Fuller loaned money to the failing Courier.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Okay, so why don't we try to, okay, we're back with Tech Stevens, January 10th, 1996, reel number one. Okay. Yeah, let's try to get the microphones closer and you know how that stuff goes. Wait, so we're talking about, we're talking about advertising and stuff, that's okay, just advertising, not advertising, we're talking about, you brought up the Dawn Patrol, why don't you continue on who was the Dawn Patrol and what it was? Well, the Dawn Patrol was started

by the Pittsburgh Courier in order to enhance the musical structure in and around the greater metropolitan area of New Orleans that everything would start around about midnight. And for all of the bands who probably played at the French Quarter, or maybe some of the other clubs in and around the city, if you go on, like Club Desire, like the Robin Hood, maybe some who played just any place, maybe the Lloyd's at Square Lounge on the West Bank of the River, or maybe on Jesse's over in Marrero, or maybe at Louis Coleman's place over on the West Bank, or either at Copper's over in Algiers. Well, most people would probably get off at midnight at that time. Some of them did, other than the ones who played until one, two, three o'clock in the morning, even at that, when they were off, they would come on this side of the river, and that's when the Dawn Patrol would really hit its feet. You know, bands, singers, Arnie Gato, Benny Espelman, just anybody, Gene Knight, Irma Thomas, they all would be there. That's when Alan Toussaint was a young man getting started coming into his own, and somehow or another, the glory of yesteryear, that was musical room in the city of New Orleans. It's all gone because the Pittsburgh Courier ceased publication back in the late 60s for the New Orleans edition anyway. So there was a fellow by the name of Fuller who loaned X numbers of dollars to the courier. He was a cosmetic salesman, and he had people working from door to door for him, but he made a lot of money at that time when people could go door to door, and he loaned some money to the courier because they were in financial straits with the coming of integration, I think, and then losing high-powered black writers and people who did the legwork for them. Well, something started happening because management was getting old, they needed the money. So what Fuller did, he failed to believe that he was a newspaper man also, but somehow or another, the Pittsburgh Courier started going down because he did not know the management skills, nor did he have the basic techniques to do journalistic writing or, shall we say, importing quality information for the readership at that time. So you started a point and what was the point? Well, about the Dawn Patrol. Well, the Dawn Patrol went from one club to the next club, and it would probably run until daylight, from midnight until daylight, as long as there was some entertainment there, something was going on. But now remember, at that time we had over 3,000 or more bars and lounges owned by black people and operated by black people. This was before integration. This was when the times began, whatever white magazines you had at the time, or jazz writers, they probably wouldn't even show up because it was segregated. And blacks had this whole volume of entertainment for themselves, which I'm sorry to say we did not have advanced electronic technical recording machines at that time to record this stuff. The ones we had, they were in the radio stations like the old WBOK, old WMRY, but you couldn't pick that stuff up to weighing .500 pounds to bring it out to record. I only wish we could have had the equipment at that time to record what actually went on. And it was a lot of fun. It went on for several years. I think it started back in 1951, 1952. My good friend, Jimmy Willis, who was the entertainment writer at that time, he was the one basically responsible for starting the Dawn Patrol because he would cover a lot of the nightlife and whatnot. I'm trying to think of the general manager at that time. Lucius Jones was the general manager for the greater metropolitan area of the Louisiana edition of Pittsburgh Courier, and he and Jimmy Willis got together, and Lucius Jones came out of that land. He was a guy who was very, very learned. He was a graduate of Morehouse University. He was very highly educated, had a beautiful command for the English language, was a tremendous award-winning writer. And they sent him down here to New Orleans to open up an office. He had an office on Dryad Street in the Louisiana Life Insurance Company building in the 1700 block of Dryad Street at that time. And by the way, the office was downstairs and upstairs was the insurance. And upstairs, this is where WMRY got started. It didn't get started there, but it started in the French Quarter. But as we started developing with Ernie the Whip, and myself, and a few other disc jockeys, then they started expanding and going out into the open black market at that time. And while we were on the radio at the time talking about the Dawn Patrol, and then playing those old 78 records at that time, that was a lot of fun. You could walk the streets of New Orleans, you didn't have all that crime. You stayed up all hours a night, and with over 3,000 or more boys in the greater metropolitan area of New Orleans, hiring from one to three young black ladies and sometimes young men. There was a lot of money in the greater metropolitan area in New Orleans for black people. And they owned a lot of things, and you had tremendous bands and singers. But who touched them? Until all of a sudden, Dave Bartholomew, who had one of the biggest bands in the city of New Orleans, a young man who had just gotten out of the service and started, and in fact he started
